en: Peṭakopadesa 3.
The Third Plane: Based on the Discourses.
Therein, what is that which is based on the discourses?
The foundation of greed, the foundation of hatred, the foundation of delusion; the foundation of non-greed, the foundation of non-hatred, the foundation of non-delusion;
the foundation of bodily action, the foundation of verbal action, the foundation of mental action;

the foundation of the faculty of faith, the foundation of the faculty of energy, the foundation of the faculty of mindfulness, the foundation of the faculty of concentration, and the foundation of the faculty of wisdom.
In this regard, what is the basis of lust?
"For a person whose thoughts are agitated,
who has intense passion, and who contemplates beauty..."
“Craving increases even further;
this indeed makes the bond tight.
“For one agitated by thought” refers to sensual lust (*kāmarāga*).
"One who contemplates beauty" refers to the basis for sensual lust.
"His craving increases further" refers to sensual craving.
"He makes this bond tight" refers to passion (*rāga*). Thus, whichever phenomenon was set down as the root, that very same phenomenon is to be understood here as well.
The Blessed One does not teach one state with reference to another state.
Whatever thought one thinks—whether it be a sensual thought—that very thought is defined by that sensual thought.
"Of one with intense lust" indicates the objective basis for that very thought.
"Craving increases further for one who contemplates the beautiful" refers to that very lust as "craving for sensual pleasure.
"He makes the bond tight" refers to that same fetter of craving.
In this way, the verses are to be inferred.
Thus it is with the Veyyākaraṇas.
Therein, the Blessed One explains a single Dhamma in three ways: by way of its outcome, its cause, and its fruit:
"One who gives becomes beloved; many resort to him."
He attains fame and his renown increases;
undaunted, he enters the assembly,
and the man who is free from stinginess becomes confident.
Whatever gift they give—this is the meritorious deed consisting in giving.
In this context, "therein" refers to the cause; "and this" refers to that which is being discussed.
Many people revere him; this is the outcome of the fact that a beautiful reputation spreads throughout the world, whereby one becomes dear and pleasing to many folk.
That one dies without remorse is the immediate result.
That one is reborn among the devas upon the breakup of the body is the fruit.
This is the foundation of greed.
In this context, what is the foundation of hatred?
"One who takes the life of a living being..."
He speaks falsehood;
he takes what is not given in the world,
and he goes unto another's wife.
And that person who is devoted to drinking fermented liquor and spirits,
without having abandoned the five enmities,
He is called "immoral";
at the breaking up of the body, that one of poor wisdom is reborn in hell.
“He who takes life” means one who, being corrupted by hatred, takes life.
“And speaks falsehood” means he speaks falsehood for the sake of harming through hatred.
“And the man who is devoted to drinking fermented and distilled liquors” means that hatred is the underlying cause.
And he who is devoted to the drinking of fermented and distilled liquors, just as one who dwells with another's wife, his enemies are provoked.
"Without abandoning the five enmities" is a designation for the transgression of the five bases of monastic life (*bhikkhāpada*);
it refers to all things born of fault. Because of that very karma produced by fault, one is called "immoral" (*dussīla*); that state, too, must be demonstrated by its cause.
And by way of its outflow and its fruit.
There are three characteristics of a fool:
he speaks ill-spoken words, he thinks ill-thought thoughts, and he performs ill-done deeds.
In this regard, that which he exerts himself in through both body and speech is his performance of wrong action.
That by which he speaks falsehood, as previously described, is his wrong speech.
And that which he intends—the mental misconduct of ill will—is his thinking of what is wrongly thought.

When one who possesses these three characteristics of a fool experiences the three corresponding kinds of pain and mental distress, it is because he speaks such talk when among a group of elders or an assembly.
Furthermore, when he engages in the ten unwholesome courses of action, such as the destruction of life, he experiences suffering and mental distress on that account.
Moreover, when he sees a thief who has committed an offense against the king, seized by the king and deprived of life, he thinks thus:
If he thinks, "Should the king find out about me as well, the king might have me seized and deprive me of life," he experiences suffering and mental distress on that account.

Furthermore, when the fool has ascended his seat, he thinks, "Whatever my destination shall be after passing away from here, beyond death," and he experiences suffering and mental distress on that account. Such is the cause for the characteristic of a fool.
The three types of suffering born thereof are the outcome.
With the breakup of the body, one is reborn in the hells; this is the fruit.
This is the section on hatred.
In this regard, what is the foundation of delusion?
"One will wander through the cycle of existence for a hundred thousand aeons."
Or even more than that,
you will go from womb to womb,
unless you take up the word of the Buddha.
“By grasping at volitional formations as self,
it is impossible that they will make an end of suffering.”
That which has entered this beginningless saṃsāra, wherein one is born and dies, has ignorance as its cause.

Furthermore, whatever purposes the volitional formations (saṅkhāras) serve, those too have ignorance as their condition; and that lack of vision regarding the word of the Buddha is pointed out in the Sutta on Ignorance itself.
Moreover, it is that which seizes the volitional formations as a self and approaches the five views regarding the five aggregates.
“This is mine, this I am, this is my self”—this sutta is placed within ignorance, deposited within ignorance.
Thus the Teacher demonstrates it by means of the sutta, by way of method, and by means of the Dhamma.
That very thing which is unique [to that context] must be demonstrated therein.
It is not otherwise.
For whatever recluses or brahmins, bhikkhus, do not understand in detail the four truths as "this is suffering," that lack of understanding therein is suffering; this is the cause.
Not understanding, one performs various volitional formations; this is the outcome.
That which clings to speculative views, thinking, "This alone is the truth; all else is vain"—this is the outflow.
That which produces renewed existence—this is the fruit.
Thus this phenomenon has been demonstrated by way of its cause, its fruit, and its outflow.
In this context, however, certain factors are common [to all].
Indeed, the "cause" (hetu) will be set forth from the very beginning in the Sutta.
For example: "Monks, there are these four ways of going to a bad destination."
In that regard, whatever one follows through favoritism and whatever one follows through fear, this is the unwholesome root of greed.
Whatever [one does] out of hatred, this is hatred itself.
Whatever [one does] out of delusion, this is delusion itself.
Thus these three unwholesome roots should be examined from the very beginning.
Where one is to be demonstrated, there one is demonstrated;
likewise two, and likewise three. For when the causes have not been set forth at the outset, neither the cause, nor the outcome, nor the fruit can be demonstrated.
And here is this verse:
“He who transgresses the Dhamma out of desire, hatred, fear, or delusion;”
“His fame diminishes,
like the moon in the dark fortnight.
Wherein this desire and greed are as previously described.
This is the foundation of delusion.
In this context, what is the foundation of non-greed?
"Dwelling contemplating foulness..."
Well-restrained in the sense faculties,
moderate in eating,
endowed with faith, and energetic;
“Māra truly cannot overcome him,
just as the wind cannot move a rocky mountain.
In this context, that investigation of the foul is the relinquishing [of sense pleasures] through seeing their danger.
"Being well-restrained in the sense-faculties" refers to the fulfillment of that very non-greed by not grasping at what causes sorrow in one's own sense-bases (*āyatana*).
"Knowing the proper measure in food" refers to the abandoning of craving for flavors.
Thus, this non-greed maintains the foundation for the contemplation of the foul; that non-greed is the cause.

By guarding the doors of the sense faculties, one maintains [the mind] from the perspective of the range of objects; by knowing the proper measure in eating, one maintains it from the perspective of external [conditions]. This is the outflow (*nissanda*).
"Māra does not overcome him, just as the wind does not move a mountain"—this is the fruit (*phala*).
Thus, the very same teaching that was set forth at the beginning is present in the middle and at the end as well.

“Monks, I do not see even a single other thing that leads so effectively to the non-arising of unarisen sensual desire, or to the abandoning of arisen sensual desire, as the sign of the unattractive (*asubhanimitta*).
For one who attends to the sign of the unattractive there, unarisen sensual desire does not arise, and arisen sensual desire is abandoned.
This is the basis for non-greed.”
Furthermore, when unarisen sensual lust is overcome by [the cultivation of] lust for the fine-material realm and lust for the immaterial realm—this is the fruit.
Thus, this state (dhamma) has been demonstrated by way of its cause, its outflow, and its fruit.
This is the exposition based on non-greed.
In this regard, what is the foundation of non-hatred?
“If one, with a mind free from hatred,
extends loving-kindness even toward a single living being, one becomes skilled thereby.”
“And the Noble One performs abundant merit by having compassion in his mind for all living beings. When one,
with a mind free from ill will, extends loving-kindness even toward a single living being, this is non-hatred (*adosa*).
"Through its eradication there is gratification; by that it becomes wholesome"—thus, one who is associated with that wholesome state enters into the designation of a state (*dhammapaññatti*).
"Wholesome" (*kusala*) is just as one is called "wise" (*pañña*) because of wisdom, or "learned" (*paṇḍita*) because of learning.
"The Noble One performs abundant merit"—this is the ripening of that very [wholesome state], and it is mundane (*lokiya*), for it is not supramundane (*lokuttara*).
In this context, that which is the practice of loving-kindness is the cause.
That he becomes skillful is the outcome.
That he generates abundant merit throughout the ground of non-affliction is the fruit.
Thus non-hatred has been demonstrated by way of its cause, its outflow, and its fruit.
There are eleven benefits of the liberation of mind through loving-kindness (*mettā-cetovimutti*).

In this context, that liberation of mind through loving-kindness is the liberation of mind through the fading away of lust for noble qualities; it is the mundane basis, and the happiness that one becomes pleasing to people in the future is the fruit. These are the eleven qualities that constitute the outflow.
And that one who has not yet completed the task is reborn in the Brahma-world:
this is the fruit.
This is the foundation of non-hatred.
In this context, what is the foundation of non-delusion?
"Wisdom is the best in the world,
that which leads to penetration;"
“By which one rightly understands the destruction of birth and death”—
this is the basis for the statement, “Wisdom is indeed supreme.”
"Penetrating" means it penetrates according to reality that which leads to Nibbāna.
"Rightly understands the destruction of birth and death" refers to non-delusion.
"Wisdom" is the cause.
That which one understands is the outflow.
That which is the destruction of birth and death is the fruit.
Thus, non-delusion is demonstrated by way of its cause, its outflow, and its fruit.
“Bhikkhus, there are these three faculties: the faculty ‘I shall come to know the unknown,’ the faculty of final knowledge, and the faculty of one who has known.
In this regard, what is the faculty ‘I shall come to know the unknown’?

Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu generates desire, exerts effort, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the direct realization of the Noble Truth of suffering that has not yet been directly realized.”
In this way, [the practice] regarding the four noble truths should be performed.
In that regard, what is the faculty of final knowledge (*aññindriya*)?
Here, monks, a monk understands as it really is: "This is the noble truth of suffering," and so on up to the path; this is the faculty of final knowledge.
Through the destruction of the taints, one becomes taintless; this is called the faculty of one who has known.
Such is this wisdom; such is its cause.
That which generates desire and exerts effort, and that which understands, is its outcome.
That by which, through the total destruction of the taints (*āsava*), the knowledge of destruction arises and the knowledge of non-arising arise—this is the outflow.
That which is Arahantship is the fruit.
Therein, "Birth is exhausted for me; the holy life has been lived; what was to be done has been done"—this is the knowledge of destruction.
"I understand: 'There is nothing further of this nature'"—this is the knowledge of non-arising.
Thus, these faculties have been demonstrated through non-delusion by way of their cause, their outflow, and their fruit.
These have been demonstrated as the uncommon [factors].
In this regard, what are the wholesome roots that are common?
Monks, I will teach you the wholesome and the wholesome roots as well.
In that context, what is the wholesome root?
Non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion.
Therein, what is the wholesome?
The eight rightnesses: from right view up to right concentration.
In this context, those which are the roots of skillfulness are the cause.
And that non-greed which gives rise to the three actions—namely, intention, effort, and concentration—is the outflow of non-greed.
In this context, that which is non-hatred is the cause.
That which establishes three qualities—right speech, right action, and right livelihood—is the outflow.
In that regard, non-delusion is the cause; that which establishes two qualities—unmistaken vision and non-proliferation—is the outflow.

As for the fruit of this holy life, it consists of those two liberations: the liberation of mind through the fading away of lust, and the liberation by wisdom through the fading away of ignorance; this is the fruit.
Thus these three roots of the wholesome have been demonstrated by way of their cause, their outflow, and their fruit.
In this manner, the common wholesome states are to be penetrated—
where there are two, and where there are three.
And here is this verse:
“The Sage relinquished both the measurable and the immeasurable arising, as well as the formative process of existence.”
"Delighting in the internal, composed,
he has shattered his own becoming like a coat of mail.
"Becomings" refers to that which is measured and that which is immeasurable, that which is reckoned as measurable and that which is reckoned as immeasurable.
In that regard, those conditioned things which are weighed—those two factors, the gratification and the danger, are weighed:
"Such is the gratification in sensual pleasures;
such is the danger in them; this is the escape from them. Thus one understands Nibbāna.
It is "incomparable" (atula) for two reasons: it is incomparable because it cannot be weighed, such that one could say, "This is so much; there is nothing beyond this";
and furthermore, it is incomparable by virtue of its marvelous nature once it has reached the state of being a jewel.
In this context, the arising of the wholesome, which is knowing and seeing, is non-delusion (*amoha*).
That which is the relinquishing of the formative forces of existence (*bhava-saṅkhāra*) once they have been known is non-greed (*alobha*).
That which is the withdrawal from distraction, expressed as "delighting within and concentrated," is non-hatred (*adosa*).
Thus, these are the three roots of the wholesome.
That which gives rise to the comparable and the incomparable is non-delusion (*amoha*).
That which is the convergence of the formations of existence (*bhava-saṅkhāra*) is greed (*lobha*); that which is the gratification of right concentrations is the cause (*hetu*).
That one who delights in the internal breaks through the eggshell of ignorance—this is the outflow.
This process of occurrence has thus been demonstrated by way of these three roots of the wholesome: by way of cause, by way of outflow, and by way of fruit.
To this extent, both this occurrence and cessation proceed by means of unwholesome roots and cease by means of wholesome roots; and herein, all unwholesome roots converge within these three.

Thus, whether it is demonstrated by way of a term such as "craving," "anger," "lack of clear comprehension," "latent tendency," "contempt," "malice," "unmindfulness," "envy," "avarice," or "ignorance," [it refers to] those things by which it is to be demonstrated.

There is no defilement for which these two statements and these lines of Dhamma have not been demonstrated; there is no defilement that enters into the convergence or inclusion within these nine categories.
This is a defilement, yet it is neither greed, nor hatred, nor delusion.
Just as the unwholesome roots are demonstrated, so too should the wholesome ones be demonstrated by way of their opposites.
This is the foundation of non-delusion.
In this context, what is the foundation of bodily action?
"One should perform wholesome deeds with the body."
Let him be restrained in body;
having abandoned bodily misconduct,
let him practice good conduct with the body.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these three kinds of good conduct.
Abstinence from the destruction of life, abstinence from taking what is not given, and abstinence from sexual misconduct—this is the basis for bodily action.
In this regard, what is the basis for verbal action?”
“The virtuous say that well-spoken speech is supreme;
one should speak the Dhamma, not what is contrary to the Dhamma—this is the second.
One should speak what is pleasant, not what is unpleasant—this is the third.”
“Speak the truth, not falsehood; this is the fourth.
These four are the good verbal conducts; this is the section on verbal action.
In that regard, what is the section on mental action?
“By means of the mind one performs wholesome karma;
one should be restrained in mind.
Having abandoned mental misconduct, [one should dwell in purity].”
"One should practice good conduct with the mind.
There are these three types of good mental conduct: non-covetousness, non-ill will, and right view; this is the basis for mental action.
These are the suttas that are not shared [with other faculties].
In this regard, what are the common discourses?
"Guarding one's speech, well-restrained in mind,
and not performing unwholesome deeds with the body;"
“One should purify these three courses of action and accomplish the path proclaimed by the Seer.
Monks, there are these three purities:
Purity of bodily action, purity of verbal action, and purity of mental action.
Therein, what is purity of bodily action?
Abstinence from taking life, abstinence from taking what is not given, and abstinence from sexual misconduct.
In this context, what is purity of verbal action?
It is abstaining from false speech …pe… abstaining from frivolous chatter.
In this context, what is purity of mental action?
It is non-covetousness, non-ill will, and right view.
This is the common sutta.
Thus, both the common suttas and the uncommon suttas are to be penetrated.
Having penetrated them, the meaning of the sutta is to be demonstrated through speech and by deed.
In this regard, what is that which is based on the faculty of faith?
“One whose faith in the Tathāgata is unshakable and well-established,
and whose virtue is noble— ”
Beloved by the noble ones and praised.
Whoever has confidence in the Sangha and a vision that is upright;
They say that for such a person life is not in vain;
indeed, faith is the source of joy and brings fulfillment.
"He has no faith," [one might say];
"Everything could be so," [said] the Blessed One—
such is the confidence in the Dhamma.
This is the foundation of the faculty of faith.
In this regard, what is the foundation of energy?
“Exert yourselves! Strive!”
Exert yourselves in the Buddha’s teaching;
shake off the army of Death as an elephant shakes down a reed-hut.
“Bhikkhus, there are these four right endeavors; this is the foundation of energy.
In that regard, what is the foundation of the faculty of mindfulness?
‘For one who possesses mindfulness, there is always good fortune.’”
“May it be well with the mindful one!
The mindful one is always better;
the mindful one attains happiness.”
The four foundations of mindfulness should be set forth in detail; this is the foundation of the faculty of mindfulness.
In that regard, what is the foundation of the faculty of concentration?
"O charioteer of men to be tamed, according to your wish..."
Neither gods nor humans, nor even all living beings together,
could know the thoughts conceived in the mind of one who dwells in peaceful, conflict-free concentration.
"Bhikkhus, there are three kinds of concentration:
with applied thought and sustained thought, without applied thought and with sustained thought only, and without applied thought and without sustained thought.
This is the foundation for the faculty of concentration."
In this context, what is the foundation of the faculty of wisdom?
"Wisdom is the best in the world," and so forth in detail.
"Monks, there are these three kinds of wisdom:"

That which consists of hearing, that which consists of reflection, and that which consists of cultivation—this is the discourse based on the faculty of wisdom. These discourses based on the faculties are unique.
In this regard, what are the discourses based on the faculties that are common?
"One who is not free from lust for sensual pleasures..."
For one whose five faculties are dull—
faith, mindfulness, energy,
serenity, and insight—
“By attacking such a bhikkhu,
one is harmed beforehand.
There are these five faculties.
The faculties such as the faculty of faith (saddhindriya) are to be understood.
A detailed discourse should be composed regarding the three types of confirmed confidence (aveccappasāda).
These are the discourses based on the faculties that are common to all.
Whatever is related to anything—whether wholesome or unwholesome—that discourse should be demonstrated by means of that specific determination; no other state (dhamma) should be demonstrated.

In this context, there is a commonality: neither exclusively wholesome nor unwholesome, such as the common wholesome roots and the common unwholesome roots; for example, "he abandons arisen sensual thought" … [etc.
… the four right efforts are both wholesome and unwholesome.
In this regard, there are these summary verses:
"For one who has applied thought, who seeks his own welfare,
and who gives, a person becomes dear."
Whoever takes the life of a living being possesses three characteristics of a fool.
Even of hundreds and thousands...
And those ascetics and brahmins who [act] out of desire,
hatred, fear, or delusion,
and through the four wrong courses.
For one who dwells contemplating foulness,
and who sees foulness even in signs—
if such a person should cherish even a single living being, [they would still be far from liberation].
If one’s friends speak what is well-spoken,
wisdom is indeed the best in the world;
it is approved as the three faculties.
The roots of the wholesome and unwholesome,
and the arising of the measurable and the immeasurable—
may one perform what is wholesome with the body.
The three types of good conduct,
and well-spoken words—
the virtuous call these the highest forms of verbal good conduct.
One should perform wholesome deeds with the body and [restrain] mental misconduct;
one should always be a protector of the body.
And the three purities:
for one who has faith in the Tathāgata,
[the path] leading to its arising is taught.
Exert yourselves, strive,
and practice right effort.
For one who possesses mindfulness, there is always good fortune.
The development of the foundations of mindfulness;
and the lack of final knowledge for one who desires it,
and the three kinds of concentration.
Wisdom is indeed the best in the world;
three kinds of wisdom have been proclaimed.
One who is not yet free from passion for sensual pleasures—
The same applies to the five faculties.
Thus ends the third section, titled "The Foundation on Sutta," in the *Peṭakopadesa* of the Elder Mahākaccāyana, the dweller in the Rose-apple Grove.
